# Best in class — the change list

**What this is, in plain terms.** On 2026-10-23 the owner read the review of Infora's library, plan, sandboxes, review cycle and context layer against the best products in the market ([the review](../reference/dms-context-review.md), [the evidence](../reference/dms-context-landscape.md)) and ruled: design the changes and build them, without the owner in the loop on each fork, and keep a clear, simply expressed list of what is being changed. This file is that list. Each change below says what a user will notice, why it is worth doing, which decisions were taken to make it buildable, and which tickets build it. The tickets live on [the board](plan.md) under the three slices named here; their records move to [plan-history.md](plan-history.md) as they close.

**Two things about how this was decided.** First, the decisions in each entry were **ruled by Claude under the owner's delegation of 2026-10-23**, not by a design session; every one is written into the ADR it touches as a dated addendum that says so, so the record stays honest about who decided what, and the owner can reopen any of them. Second, no mockups were drawn: the design lifecycle's purpose for a mockup is to give the owner something to rule on, and the owner has waived that step for this work, so the screens were designed straight on the design tokens and are photographed into the walkthrough when built. Nothing here touches the ruled foundations the review found ahead of the market: the ethical wall, the rule that private knowledge steers but never grounds, record state, the plan-first discipline, immutable versions and the review cycle's two gates.

**Order.** Three slices, built in this order, each a named slice on the board: **Register** (the structural fixes a pilot user feels in week one), **Reach** (what the AI read, and what it could not), **Working together** (the plan, the sandbox and the review as shared work). The pilot deployment slice stays on the board; the owner's ruling of 2026-10-23 puts this work ahead of it.

---

## Slice Register — the document record and the register

**1. One lifecycle vocabulary, shown the same way everywhere.** Every row and page shows two small badges: where the document is (Working v0.3, Frozen for QA, QA accepted, Promoted P01, In review, Responding, Accepted C01, Superseded, Withdrawn, Rejected) and whether the AI may use it and why not. Today each screen uses its own words and the plan and library say "Suitability" where the record ruled "status code". *Why:* a user should never have to translate between screens. *Decided:* the labels come from one table keyed to `CONTEXT.md`'s four axes; the default schema's "Suitability code" field and the library column are relabelled "Status code". *Builds as:* T-455.

**2. Doors for what is already built.** Sandbox version history with restore and undelete; removing a document from the library and purging it; loading and retiring the firm's drafting manual; sharing a deliverable with an organisation or a named person; "who can see this" on every document. The API has all of these and no screen reaches them. *Why:* capability the record says exists and a user cannot find is the same as missing. *Decided:* nothing new; each is already ruled (ADR-0032, 0033, 0048, 0050, 0054). *Builds as:* T-456.

**3. One document page.** Every deliverable gets a single page with tabs: Overview, Versions, Relationships, Review record, Transmittals, Activity. The plan row, the library row, the review list, a citation chip and the side menu all land on it. The four partial views in use today (the plan modal, the library modal, the review status page's facts, the side menu's text modal) retire into it. *Why:* a document controller asks "what is this and what happened to it" a hundred times a day and today gets four different partial answers. *Decided:* the page is read-only; quick edits happen in the register's side panel (change 4); access is unchanged, per deliverable, per organisation. *Builds as:* T-457, T-458.

**4. The register grammar.** The plan, the library, the sandbox's all-documents view and the review list share one table: a search box that searches reference, title and content through the same index the AI uses; filter chips (discipline, document type, status code, record state, AI reach, producer, reviewer, date); a column chooser; sort on any column; saved views with a name, private or shared within the organisation; row selection with a bulk-action bar (transmit, issue externally, propose supersede, classify with an explicit append-or-replace choice, export the selection to Excel); a side panel on row select for the quick edits now in modals; one row menu instead of five inline actions. Reference material gets a title and the same columns. *Why:* every incumbent has a searchable register with bulk edit; Infora's library is a fixed-order list. *Decided:* a saved view is a named filter, never an access object (new `CONTEXT.md` term); people search the agent's index, access-resolved identically; the plan's organisation-standard locked columns stay as ruled, personal views may hide but not add. *Builds as:* T-459 (search and paging endpoints), T-460 (the register component and saved views), T-461 (bulk actions and export), T-462 (the three screens moved onto it).

**5. Scale readiness.** The register endpoints page and sort on the server, the search is index-backed from the start, and the operating envelope states the ceiling and a revisit trigger. *Why:* today the library returns every row and the screen renders them all; the ontology was designed to scale retrieval to a hundred thousand documents and the register would not keep up. *Decided:* a revisit trigger in `operating-envelope.md`. *Builds as:* inside T-459.

**6. The AI transparency table.** A "How the AI works here" page in project settings and the workspace: one row per AI feature saying what it reads, what it may write, where it runs, what it keeps and for how long, that it never trains, and a per-project switch the owner's super user can turn off, audited. A switched-off feature is absent from every launcher, not greyed. *Why:* an owner organisation asks exactly this on day one, and the answer today is spread across six ADRs; Bluebeam publishes the best such table in the market. *Decided:* the switch sits beneath the deployment tier and only narrows, never widens, reach (ADR-0037 note); the change is audited like a rails change (ADR-0030). *Builds as:* T-463.

**7. Copy and vocabulary.** One short line under each heading with a "learn more" that opens the longer explanation; the six disabled placeholder chips removed from the composer and the three placeholder rail items removed from the workspace until the thing behind them works; "Personal workspace" and "Personal sandbox" made one word. *Why:* the record's register had leaked into the interface; nobody reads a paragraph under a heading twice, and a control that does nothing teaches people to stop clicking. *Decided:* design-rules §G gains the check "every label is a `CONTEXT.md` term or a plain verb". *Builds as:* T-464.

**8. Undo and feedback.** A toast with Undo for every reversible act (withdraw by its maker, move, rename, bind, classification, bulk edits), skeleton loading on every register, and optimistic updates on rename, move and bind with rollback on refusal. *Why:* reversibility that is not offered at the moment of the act does not feel reversible. *Builds as:* T-465.

**9. A real command palette, and keyboard moves.** ⌘K finds any document by reference or title, jumps to any section and runs the current row's actions, with a visible hint; J and K move through review comments, R replies, E marks addressed; F opens filters in a register; "?" shows the shortcuts. Today the ⌘K hint is wired to nothing. *Builds as:* T-466.

**10. The home page as a work queue.** Project home becomes "waiting on you" (appointments to accept, submissions to acknowledge, rounds to close, responses to write, proposals to decide, relationships to confirm, open findings and gaps on your drafts, re-checks due, milestones overdue), recent documents and your saved views; the workspace home does the same across projects. *Why:* the things a person is waiting to do are spread across five screens today. *Builds as:* T-467.

## Slice Reach — what the AI read, and what it could not

**11. Citations land on the passage.** Hovering a citation shows the cited passage with its document, revision, page and record state; clicking opens the document page scrolled to it, highlighted. Authority citations become clickable. The passage text is always read from the stored chunk the run recorded, never produced by a model, and a scanned document whose text could not be extracted is marked as not citable on its row and in the reach statement. A quoted rule in a finding gets its own visibly different card, never a citation chip. *Why:* a citation that opens a whole document is a citation nobody checks; the research shows people trust citations even when they are wrong, so the check must be one hover. *Decided:* `Q-022` closes; ADR-0022 gains the note that a citation renders its recorded chunk, never re-retrieved. *Builds as:* T-468.

**12. The scope control and the reach statement.** One control, used by Ask, the document creator, the checker and the editor: a searchable picker with facets from the classification vocabulary, explicit documents, and saved scopes. The chosen scope is written on the run's plan before anything is retrieved. Every answer and draft then says in plain words what was read and what was left out and why: "Read 14 documents in your scope. Excluded: 2 superseded, 1 awaiting re-check, 1 not citable (scan). Your scope left out 31 you could have included." It never counts what the wall hides. *Why:* no product in the market shows what was out of reach; Infora can, because it filters before it retrieves. *Decided:* `Q-028` ruled as the tracker recommended (declared, auditable, pre-retrieval, visible, never implicit); ADR-0029 gains the scope on the request; ADR-0018 gains the note that a reach statement counts only what the requester may see and what state excluded. New `CONTEXT.md` terms: Scope, Reach statement. *Builds as:* T-469 (scope on the request and the pre-filter wired), T-470 (the control and the statement).

**13. The sandbox working set.** A user may pick, from a searchable picker, documents from sandboxes they are in and pin them to a run as labelled, uncitable background; answers that lean on them say "drawing on your working area" and never cite them; the set is visible on the run and in the shared thread to the sandbox's participants only; nothing is ever pinned automatically. The checker already has this picker; it becomes the one control everywhere and replaces the editor's raw-id field. *Why:* the daily question is "given my three drafts and the library, what have we missed", and every product users know lets them ask it. *Decided:* `Q-020` ruled by an ADR-0022 addendum: sandbox material enters a run only as a user-chosen working set on the attached-source terms. New term: Working set. *Builds as:* T-471.

**14. Reference material intake and currency.** The owner uploads reference material from the library screen, in bulk, with progress; each file lands in an intake queue where the AI proposes a title, document type, discipline and the other facets and the owner confirms, singly or in bulk, before anything grounds; each reference row then carries "confirmed current by" and "re-check due", a due re-check goes to the owner's work queue, and a document nobody has confirmed current keeps grounding with that fact shown on every citation of it. *Why:* reference material arrives today only by an operator's command line, with no title, no classification and no currency; Box and Glean show the intake and verify loop. *Decided:* stale reference material keeps grounding, marked, with the re-check in the queue (silence is worse than a dated answer, and withdrawal exists for the known-wrong case); ADR-0011 addendum for the lifecycle; ADR-0045's agent-proposed classification deferral is split and the reference-material half built now; the confirmer's name joins the personal-data register. *Builds as:* T-472 (upload and intake), T-473 (currency and re-check).

**15. Supersede impact.** When the owner supersedes, withdraws or re-issues a library document, the dialog shows the owner what the owner may already see (library versions that reference it, and the owner's own drafts and runs); on confirmation every organisation whose drafts, versions or past answers cited it is told by a notification pointing at its own affected documents; the editor and the checker raise a "stale grounding" finding on each affected sentence. Impact is computed per organisation and never aggregated across the wall. *Why:* only Infora's data can answer "what else relied on this", and nobody else in the market handles stale content well. *Decided:* pulled forward from the deferred ontology slice as a deterministic check over the audit; a fourth pilot notification event, "a document you cited was superseded" (ADR-0049); a new finding kind, "stale grounding" (ADR-0048, 0053); an accepted chapter's record state is unchanged and the stale citation is shown on its page for the next revision. *Builds as:* T-474.

**16. Visible gaps, and passage authorship.** Where the record cannot support a drafted sentence, the agent's proposed draft carries a typed gap marker in its place ("Gap: the record does not give the made-ground thickness per parcel"), which lands only through the suggestion the person accepts; an open gap blocks promotion like an open finding; every passage shows on hover who drafted it (a person, or the agent in a named run) and who accepted it, and an export appendix can list the machine-drafted passages. *Why:* a plausible sentence with a citation is trusted even when wrong, so the honest signal is an explicit gap; the newest drafters (Avoice's "TBC", Alloovium's authorship tracking) do this. *Decided:* ADR-0048 addendum: the gap marker is the one non-prose element the drafting side may propose, landing only through an accepted suggestion, with §3 unchanged; ADR-0049: open gaps join open threads and findings as a promotion block. New term: Gap marker. *Builds as:* T-475.

**17. Findings polish, and three rules from the checkers.** Severity and kind filters with counts; a table view of findings for long documents; both sides of a two-place finding opened side by side; the rule "a judgement finding with no passage and no rule is not raised", enforced in code; a strength map on the launcher saying which rule kinds are settled in code and which rest on a model's reading; and an optional disproving pass for judgement findings, a second call per finding that tries to show it wrong, declared in the plan with its cost shown before the run and its removals counted in the coverage statement. *Why:* the best drawing and spec checkers cite both sides of every finding, refuse a finding without a citation, and say what they are weak at. *Decided:* the disproving pass is a launcher option, off by default, so the plan stays computed in code (ADR-0053 addendum). *Builds as:* T-476.

## Slice Working together — the plan, the sandbox and the review as shared work

**18. Sandbox collaboration.** Presence on sandbox rows and in the editor's top bar; a dot on a document changed since you last opened it; a History panel on every document (every working version, who and when, restore with confirmation, frozen ones named); upload lands in the selected sandbox and folder with a progress list, instead of dropping into the default sandbox; inline rename; a "Request internal review" dialog that freezes, names the QA reviewer and adds a note in one step; the lifecycle badge beside the document name in the editor. *Why:* the parts are correct and the connective tissue is missing. *Decided:* nothing new; freeze, the working series and multiplayer are ruled (ADR-0032, 0039, 0041). *Builds as:* T-477, T-478.

**19. Review polish.** A threads panel listing every comment with its state (open, answered, no change, overtaken by a later version), filterable by reviewer and code, with the keyboard moves; a progress line per reviewer, visible to the reviewing side while a round is open as ADR-0052 allows; a response's "revised passage" becomes a link that opens the next version scrolled to the change; a Compare tab on the document page showing two authored versions side by side in the tracked-change styles, and two PDFs side by side for uploaded ones; a reviewer filter for the authoring team's response sweep. *Why:* GitHub, Google Docs and Word taught reviewers these moves. *Decided:* nothing new; `Q-038` stays open. *Builds as:* T-479, T-480.

**20. The plan as the owner's schedule.** A plan row may carry milestones (a target date and the status code it must reach by then); the owner's schedule gains a coverage view across planned, bound, frozen, QA accepted, promoted, in review and accepted, with overdue and "no draft bound yet" flagged and a one-line summary; the plan exports to Excel in the shape it imports; overdue milestones reach the work queue. *Why:* the plan is already the single record the MIDP tools try to build; it lacks the time axis and the view. *Decided:* ADR-0008 addendum: milestones on the plan row, set by the producing organisation, read by the owner; status-code milestones follow the National Annex; the template export and batch import stay create-only and gain the milestone columns. *Builds as:* T-481.

---

**Not changed, on purpose.** Access per status code, folders as access objects, auto-sharing on add, numeric confidence scores, a content health score as a verdict, a user-facing model picker, Figma's all-or-nothing review, a graph explorer, scripted rules, event-triggered agent runs, outside assistants with direct access to project material, vendor staff inside the loop, memory across sessions, and agents that file without a review step. The reasons are in the review's §4.

**What is left for the owner.** Nothing is blocked on the owner. Two things are worth a look when convenient: the record of each ruling in the ADR addenda, any of which can be reopened in a design session; and the walkthrough once each slice is photographed, because the owner is the product's first tester.
